site.title: bench
site.description: Run a team of coding agents without losing track of what they are doing.

pages.title: bench — run a team of coding agents, stay in control
pages.description: Your agents ship faster than you can keep track. Every task is a card, every agent gets its own worktree, every change waits as a PR. Nothing merges without you.

pages.title: Install and first run
pages.description: Untar bench into .task-manager/, run start.sh, and answer the two questions the first run asks.

pages.title: Install outside the application
pages.description: The other install: the tool in one directory, the tickets in a repository of their own, and the application untouched except by the code the agents write.
pages.lede: The same board, installed beside the application instead of inside it — what to run, which flags there are, and which of the two git identities each thing belongs to.
pages.to: ## Set up with your coding agent

pages.title: Set up Bench with your coding agent
pages.description: bootstrap.py looks first, previews every change, makes them only when you approve, and hands you the board's address — with instructions bounded enough to give to a coding agent.
pages.lede: The guided way into an external install: what to paste into your coding agent, the three commands it runs, the choices that stay yours, and where setup continues once the board is up.
pages.from: ## Set up with your coding agent

pages.title: The five stages
pages.description: backlog, to-do, in-progress, review, done — the directory a task file sits in is its status, and there is no other source of truth.

pages.title: Task files
pages.description: A task is a markdown file with a numbered name and a short header. Status is the only field the board enforces.

pages.title: Claiming a card
pages.description: Claiming is moving: taking a card towards work is the commitment, and that is where ownership is recorded.

pages.title: Agents on the board
pages.description: Start work makes a worktree and a branch, runs the agent headless, and moves the card on the way it exits.

pages.title: Execution plans
pages.description: Which branch a card's work starts from and which branch its PR targets, resolved and validated before anything is created, then recorded with the run.
pages.lede: Bench owns the git lifecycle, so it decides it once: where a card's work starts, what its PR targets, what selected each, what refuses before a branch or a worktree exists, and why the answer stops moving after the launch.

pages.title: Profiles and approved context
pages.description: What a run may do in the checkout bench prepared, and which files it is guaranteed to have read — resolved, hashed and recorded before a model is invoked.
pages.lede: A plan says which checkout a run works in. This is the other half of the same decision: the named commands it may launch, the inputs pinned read-only for it, how strongly each of those actually holds, and the manifest that says what this particular run rode.
pages.to: ## From evidence to merge: the whole journey

pages.title: From evidence to merge
pages.description: Checks, review and merge requirements in plain words, the one recommended verification route, what each extra assurance buys, and the journey from a card's first commit to its merge, counted.
pages.lede: Before the reference pages: what a check, a review and a merge requirement each are, the single setup most projects need, why a pass is reused only when bench can prove it is the same check, and what one legacy record still costs.
pages.from: ## From evidence to merge: the whole journey

pages.title: Verification
pages.description: Your team provides the tests and checking programs. Bench runs approved checks, records their results and enforces the requirements you configure.
pages.lede: Verification means checking the work, not taking an agent's word for it. Learn what your team needs to supply, what Bench does for you, and why a passing check is only as useful as what it tests.
pages.to: ## Gates: nothing merges on a report

pages.title: Gates
pages.description: May this merge happen? Required checks and review policies per guarded mutation, answered from evidence bound to the exact commit about to move.
pages.lede: A clean exit, new commits and a quiet CI are the three things that used to answer this, and not one of them is evidence. What a gate requires instead, where it is enforced, why a COMMENTED review is never an approval, and what an override records.
pages.from: ## Gates: nothing merges on a report
pages.to: ## Delivery status: one answer per card

pages.title: Delivery status
pages.description: One answer per card, computed on the server: what is happening, the one next action and who holds it, and the merge requirements that apply at the current commit — drawn the same on the card, its Overview and the merge dialog.
pages.lede: The card face, the Overview and the merge dialog used to work out a card's status each for itself, and could disagree. Now the server answers once and every surface draws that answer: what it says, what reading it costs (nothing), and what it never decides.
pages.from: ## Delivery status: one answer per card

pages.title: Readiness
pages.description: What this board would grant, run and refuse — asked without paying for a model, at four honest distances, with every diagnostic's remedy.
pages.lede: An operator used to find a mistyped policy the expensive way: move a card, click start work, watch the run refuse. The doctor answers the same questions in milliseconds, and says how far each answer is from the thing you actually care about.
pages.to: ## Settings: reading the configuration, and changing it safely

pages.title: Settings
pages.description: How this bench is configured, what has actually been verified, and what to configure next — read from the resolvers that already answer for it, and changed through validate, preview and an explicit apply.
pages.lede: Everything bench resolves was configuration an operator set up in a JSON document and read back in a terminal. The Settings view is the same facts in one place, in words, with the distinction between them kept — and the one file it edits is written atomically, over the exact revision the editor was shown.
pages.from: ## Settings: reading the configuration, and changing it safely

pages.title: Links to views and cards
pages.description: Every card, card section, phase, session and Settings section has an address: open it in a new tab, refresh it, share it, and Back and Forward walk them.
pages.lede: The board's address bar follows what you are looking at. Which addresses there are, what names a card or a session in one, how history behaves, and what the page says when a destination is archived or not there — opening an address only ever reads.
pages.from: ## Addresses: a link to every view and card

pages.title: PRs and review
pages.description: A card entering review gets a PR opened for it by the board; then review PR, copilot and act on PR, until it settles.
pages.to: ## Refining a card: comments and agent-proposed edits

pages.title: Refining a card
pages.description: Comment on a card, ask an agent to propose a revised brief, read the diff, then apply or discard it. Refining a card is not implementing it.
pages.from: ## Refining a card: comments and agent-proposed edits

pages.title: Phases
pages.description: A phase is a card that lists its cards: Type: Phase, a ## Cards section in run order, and membership that runs one direction only.
pages.lede: The model, before anything runs: what a phase card is made of, how membership is written down, why it runs one direction only, and what the board flags when the list does not resolve.
pages.to: ### A phase runs on a branch of its own

pages.title: Running a phase
pages.description: Move the phase card into To Do and the Orchestrator queues it and its members: each branches from the phase's tip, is integrated in turn, and one PR goes into main at the end.
pages.lede: Everything between queueing a phase and the one PR it ends with: the one move that queues it, where each member's branch is cut, what a member waits on, what refuses a merge, and what merging the phase does to the cards it carried.
pages.from: ### A phase runs on a branch of its own
pages.to: ### A phase's members leave the Board view

pages.title: Where a phase is drawn
pages.description: The Board stops listing a phase's members and the phase card stands for them; the Phases view gives every phase a swimlane of its own.
pages.lede: A phase card stands for cards the kanban no longer lists. What the columns say instead, what the phase card owes in return, and the view that gives every phase a lane of its own.
pages.from: ### A phase's members leave the Board view

pages.title: Delegate work to an orchestrator
pages.description: You stay the product owner; an orchestrator runs the cards you moved into To Do — agents, checks, an independent review, repair and an allowed merge — under an agreement you apply, with every step written on the card.
pages.lede: What changes when you hand the clicking to an orchestrator: a worked example from a teammate's idea to a merged card, what you decide and where, what it never does, how to turn it on, and the sixteen decisions it is built on.
pages.from: ### Start here: you own the product, the orchestrator runs the project
pages.to: ### Operating agreements, scopes and one installation

pages.title: Agreements and ownership
pages.description: The operating agreement: what each scope may do and how much, narrowed from Bench to phase; one designated installation; and the last mover — not the last editor — deciding whose a card is.
pages.lede: The foundation every orchestrated action asks first: the agreement in force and its defaults, how a phase can only narrow its parent, which installation may execute, and how a card's latest attributable move decides whether it is yours to orchestrate.
pages.from: ### Operating agreements, scopes and one installation
pages.to: ### Orchestrator reasoning: launched agents, public responses

pages.title: Reasoning and decisions
pages.description: Every judgement is a launched coding-agent job given the card's context by exact reads, answering in a validated public response; its questions, your answers and its records live on the card.
pages.lede: How an orchestrator thinks without a hidden model loop: the read-only reason intent, what context it is pinned, the response contract and what is refused, and the card's own record of questions, answers, blockers and actions.
pages.from: ### Orchestrator reasoning: launched agents, public responses

pages.title: Scheduling and recovery
pages.description: Bounded passes over a durable operation ledger: dependencies, first-come-first-served admission and declared overlap, capacity reserved before a launch, crash windows reconciled, failures classified — and stalled work diagnosed, never killed for silence.
pages.lede: What a pass does and what it never does twice: how work is chosen, how an intent and a receipt make a restart safe, what is retried and what is held for you, and how a stalled or failed run is diagnosed within a fixed number of attempts.
pages.to: ### Delivery: checks, independent review, repair and your merge policy

pages.title: Delivery and phase scopes
pages.description: Checks at the exact head, a review by a different model, bounded repair and a merge only under your rules — and a phase scope that integrates its members and delivers the integrated head.
pages.lede: From a card in Review to Done without a click of yours, and the same for a phase: what independent review has to prove, why ungated is never called verified, how uncertain merges reconcile, and why a member integrated into its phase branch is not delivered.
pages.from: ### Delivery: checks, independent review, repair and your merge policy

pages.title: Ask the orchestrator
pages.description: Ask why work is or is not moving — about the board, a phase or a card — and get an evidence-linked answer from one read-only reasoning run, kept as a synced conversation. Asking explains; it never acts.
pages.lede: How to ask from the Orchestrator or a card, what the run reads and how fresh it is, what an answer holds, what it costs and who may ask, where replies are kept, and the line between asking and acting.

pages.title: Exact Brain changes
pages.description: Review a Brain Agent update against the exact revision it was drafted from, then View changes: the entry opened on each changed passage, with Previous and Next, saved, committed and shared said apart, and an honest historical diff once the entry has moved on.
pages.lede: What the review shows before Apply, the change record an Apply keeps and where it lives, how View changes places each change — exactly, relocated or not at all — and what reading it does: nothing.
pages.from: ### Reviewing and navigating exact Brain changes

pages.title: Comments on selected Brain text
pages.description: Select a passage of a Brain entry to comment on it or ask the Brain Agent to work on it: anchored to the entry's Markdown, located conservatively after edits, kept as versioned history in the work state, and resolved only by an applied edit that touched the passage or by a person.
pages.lede: How a selection becomes an anchor and when it is refused, what In place, Found again, Outdated and Detached mean, why Post comment starts nothing and Ask agent starts exactly one drafting request, what resolves a thread and what keeps it open, and the record it is all kept in.

pages.title: The shared agent conversation
pages.description: One right-hand panel for every agent purpose beside the work — Orchestrator questions, Brain drafts, seed and evaluation drafts, card refinement and runs to inspect: its target inferred from where you asked, kept with your unsent text across navigation and reload, and launching nothing until you submit.
pages.lede: Where the panel opens and what it is about, why a conversation follows its target and never the page, what leads and what folds away, what each purpose supports — follow-up, cancel, reporting — and what opening, closing and reloading do: nothing.

pages.title: Agent activity and the inbox
pages.description: The header's Activity control and its inbox: what every agent is doing or has done, projected from records bench already keeps, with unread results and questions kept across navigation, reload and restart — and nothing marked read, opened or launched by looking.
pages.lede: Which records the list reads and the state words it uses, what makes a transition unread and what acknowledges it, why a proposal is never applied and applied is never shared, how optional browser notifications behave, and where the inbox is kept, for whom and for how long.

pages.title: The Orchestrator view
pages.description: One place to read and steer orchestration — questions to the orchestrator, the decision trace, work, decisions, phases, recovery, activity and the agreement — and what the end-to-end tests prove about all of it, and what stays yours.
pages.lede: Where a person reads and acts on everything orchestration does: the nine sections and their actions, the decision trace that says why it acted or waited, the ways in from the Board and a card, then what the cross-layout journeys prove, what they cannot, and the maintenance acts that stay a person's.

pages.title: Team mode
pages.description: BOARD_SYNC makes origin/main the truth and every board a converging replica: moves commit and push themselves, and a beat pulls what the other boards published.

pages.title: External workspaces
pages.description: Four roots named separately and two git identities kept apart: the tool, the application, the work state and the worktrees, with tickets that never reach the application's history.
pages.lede: What changes when bench stops living in the repository it manages: which of the four locations holds what, which repository each operation belongs to, how far the tickets are versioned, where a card's branch is planned, and why a layout that does not hold together is refused rather than worked around.

pages.title: Operating an external install
pages.description: Hooks that reach an agent without a tracked file, a record that names where things really are, and start, stop and update each knowing which board is theirs.
pages.lede: Living with an external install: giving your own sessions live visibility without writing into the application, what the record says about where the tickets are, what is never thrown away, and running a candidate bench from a stable operator install.

pages.title: The three-layer law
pages.description: Core knows tasks, worktrees, PRs and events. Drivers know apps, adapters know agent vendors, local/ knows your project.

pages.title: Agent adapters
pages.description: Headless jobs run through an adapter, so the board works with coding agents other than Claude Code — and never sees a vendor's payloads.
pages.lede: The adapter is the layer that knows a coding agent. It launches one headless job, and translates that vendor's events into the board's own schema — which is what keeps every other line of core free of any particular agent.

pages.title: Settings
pages.description: Every BOARD_* setting with its default and what changing it does — generated from manager/core/.env.example, which is where the defaults live.
pages.lede: The whole of manager/core/.env.example, read out of the file itself on every build. Precedence runs process environment, then your manager/local/.env, then the defaults below — so a key you never copied is a key at the value shown here.

pages.title: The adapter contract
pages.description: The two executables an adapter is — run and wire — the three launch intents, the model passthrough, and the normalized event schema.
pages.lede: What you implement to put a different coding agent behind the board. Two executables, three launch intents, and one event schema; the shipped claude/ and opencode/ adapters are both of these read side by side.

pages.title: The driver contract
pages.description: manager/local/driver/start: the executable that launches your app from a task's worktree, and the four things the board asks of it.
pages.lede: How an app starts is project knowledge, so the board does not hold any of it: it runs one executable you write and owns it as a process group. Four env vars in, one line out when the app is up, and SIGTERM to park it.
pages.to: ## The activity bar and the archive

pages.title: The local-command contract
pages.description: manager/local/commands/: project chores run against a task's worktree, surfaced as chips on the cards that have a branch.
pages.lede: The driver's contract again, for the chores that belong to one checkout rather than to the app: migrations, reseeds, asset rebuilds. An executable in manager/local/commands/ becomes a chip on every card with a branch.

pages.title: Not found
pages.description: That path is not a page on this site.
